summary: Suggests an addressing scheme for using the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) in the Internet, as a solution to a problem with "ISO-grams". It revises RFC 986 and invited discussion.

plainLanguage.summary: Two sets of networking rules used different address labels. This memo shows how to match them up so they can share the same network.

how long is an internet clnp address
subtitle: A 20-octet address layout for carrying ISO CLNP traffic across the Internet, with room for IP addresses inside.

tldr.problem: ISO addressing for the Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) is very flexible, so a specific address format had to be chosen before ISO traffic could be routed through the Internet.
tldr.mechanism: Addresses are 20 octets with a fixed prefix (AFI 47, ICD 0006, version 02), a global area number, a routing domain number, padding, an IGP-specific part and a selector.
tldr.outcome: The memo revises and obsoletes RFC 986. It proposes the scheme as a protocol for the Internet community and asks for discussion.

today: RFC 1069 obsoletes RFC 986. The unit metadata lists its status as Unknown and shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The memo itself only proposed the scheme and asked for discussion.

sections.title: Objectives
sections.content:
The memo suggests an addressing scheme for the ISO Connectionless Network Protocol (CLNP) in the Internet, as a solution to one of the problems of using "ISO-grams" there. The authors see two ways to bring ISO protocols to the Internet: put ISO applications on top of the IP transport function, or integrate the whole ISO stack without merging the two suites. The second route relies on CLNP and IP being very similar in function, so some or all Internet gateways could become multiprotocol.

The open problem is that the ISO network layer addressing standard allows a great deal of flexibility, so one address format has to be chosen. The scheme also has to serve routing domains that use addresses derived from IP addresses, routing domains that follow the ANSI and ISO intra-domain routing protocol being developed, and a future inter-domain routing protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: To let two kinds of mail systems share one postal network, everyone has to agree how to write the address on the envelope.

sections.title: Routing Domains
sections.content:
The scheme uses the ANSI and ISO idea of a routing domain. It is similar to, but not identical with, an Internet autonomous system: a domain includes gateways, networks and end systems, and its boundaries can define access control and policy routing. Like autonomous systems, routing domains may be assumed to be topologically contiguous. Routing domains for ISO IP need not relate to existing autonomous system assignments.

The RFC expects the scheme to suit long-term use, but also expects the Internet to be interconnected with domains that use other schemes, such as addresses assigned through ANSI or by national standards organizations. Gateways will then have to route to destinations that do not follow this format. Assigning routing domain identifiers is an assigned-numbers function that is out of scope for the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: A routing domain is like a neighborhood with its own local street rules, but with a shared way to name the neighborhood so outsiders can find it.

sections.title: The Address Layout
sections.content:
An Internet CLNP address is 20 octets. It starts with a one-octet Authority and Format Identifier (AFI) of 47, which marks an ISO-6523-ICD assignment, followed by the two-octet Initial Domain Identifier, the International Code Designator 0006 assigned to the Internet. The rest is the Domain Specific Part (DSP).

The DSP holds a one-octet version number that must be 02, a two-octet global area number (reserved for now, and must be zero), a two-octet routing domain number, a variable-length padding field that must be zero, an IGP-specific part and a one-octet selector. The padding makes the whole address 20 octets. The selector does the job of the IP user protocol field, because ISO treats identifying the user protocol as an addressing matter.

The routing domain number may be that of any gateway through which the host is directly reachable. Selector values and domain identifiers are left to the Assigned Numbers authority.
sections.plainLanguage: The address is a fixed-length label. The first part says what kind of label it is, the middle says which neighborhood, and the last bits say which house and which door.

sections.title: Inside the IGP-Specific Field
sections.content:
A routing domain may use any addressing scheme in the IGP-specific part, up to 11 octets, which keeps the address within the 20-octet maximum. Two formats are expected at first.

For domains that route internally with IP addresses, the four-octet Internet address is encoded in octets 16 to 19, after padding in octets 9 to 15. For domains following the draft ANSI intra-domain routing proposal, the address uses a LOC-AREA field (octets 12 and 13) and an ID field (octets 14 to 19), with padding in octets 9 to 11.

Isolated end systems and simple LANs that reach the Internet only through public data networks may use a separate address format based on their X.121 address. These are handled like addresses from domains that use other formats.
sections.plainLanguage: Each neighborhood may write its local house numbers however it likes, as long as they fit in the space the big label leaves for them.

sections.title: Migration to Future Routing Protocols
sections.content:
At first, routing of ISO datagrams may treat the first 8 octets of the address (AFI, ICD, version, global area number and routing domain number) as a flat field naming the routing domain. If EGP is used between routing domains, a new version of EGP may be needed to carry 8-octet routing domain numbers instead of 3-octet network numbers.

The authors expect the number of networks to grow until no gateway can keep a route to every one, so routing by routing domain instead of by network is a necessary long-term step. The global area field is provided in case the number of routing domains grows too large as well. In the long term, routing will need variable-length routing domain identifiers, using either an address mask or a length field. The details of such a protocol are out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: When there are too many streets to remember, you route by neighborhood first. If there get to be too many neighborhoods, you group those into bigger areas.

fields.desc: International Code Designator assigned to the Internet.

fields.desc: Reserved; must be zero for now.

fields.desc: Octets 16 to 19; the IP address of the end system.

fields.desc: Plays the role of the IP user protocol field.
